claim: The Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 removed CAB authority over routes and rates and enabled the widespread adoption of hub-and-spoke networks after 1978.
source_title: Airline Deregulation Act
supporting_excerpt: The Airline Deregulation Act... removed the Civil Aeronautics Board from overseeing 'routes, rates, and service' by setting schedules and fares... After deregulation, the airlines quickly moved to a hub-and-spoke system.
caveat: Wikipedia secondary source; underlying primary is 49 U.S.C. § 1371 et seq. as amended.

claim: Since 1978, the US airline industry has experienced 45 mergers and 212 bankruptcies, arriving at a four-major structure (Delta, United, American, Southwest).
source_title: How To Fix Flying in the U.S.
supporting_excerpt: In reality, deregulation has produced 45 mergers and 212 bankruptcies. The airline industry today is characterized by... consolidation to four main airlines.
caveat: Secondary count; not a primary DOT source. Order of magnitude reliable, exact count depends on definition of 'merger'.

claim: Braniff International ceased flight operations May 12, 1982 and filed Chapter 11 the same night, following post-deregulation overexpansion and a fuel-cost spike.
source_title: Debt-Ridden Braniff Airline Files for Bankruptcy
supporting_excerpt: Debt-Ridden Braniff Airline Files for Bankruptcy... The airline was grounded by post-deregulation overexpansion.
caveat: Historical newspaper record.

claim: Pittsburgh's Midfield Terminal opened October 1, 1992 at a construction cost of approximately $1 billion, designed with an X-shaped airside optimized for US Airways' connecting-hub operations.
source_title: Across the Aisle from Pittsburgh Airport's Executive Director on Pittsburgh's Rise and Fall as a Hub (Part 1)
supporting_excerpt: The new midfield terminal opened October 1, 1992... designed specifically for US Airways' hub operations with an X-shaped configuration.
caveat: Secondary but sourced to airport-executive interview.

claim: US Airways closed its Pittsburgh hub in 2004 after unsuccessful negotiations to lower airport fees; cost per enplaned passenger rose to nearly $15 in 2011, almost twice what airlines paid in 2002.
source_title: Across the Aisle from Pittsburgh Airport's Executive Director on Pittsburgh's Rise and Fall as a Hub (Part 1)
supporting_excerpt: US Airways closed its hub in 2004 after a cost dispute with the airport... The cost per enplaned passenger rose to nearly $15 in 2011, almost twice what airlines paid in 2002.
caveat: Secondary source; airport-executive interview.

claim: Pittsburgh International effectively operated 'a hub airport 21 years after the hub left,' with its terminal geometry ultimately requiring a landside replacement.
source_title: Pittsburgh Ran a Hub Airport 21 Years After the Hub Left
supporting_excerpt: Pittsburgh Ran a Hub Airport 21 Years After the Hub Left.
caveat: Commentary framing, useful as a lesson-header rather than a data point.

claim: Pittsburgh International opened a new $1.75 billion landside terminal in 2025, effectively replacing the connecting-hub geometry of the 1992 building.
source_title: Pittsburgh Airport cuts ribbon on $1.75 billion terminal
supporting_excerpt: Pittsburgh Airport cuts ribbon on $1.75 billion terminal.
caveat: Regional news source; cost figure widely reported.

claim: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport handled 22.7 million passengers in 2005 at its peak as Delta's second-largest hub, with 600+ daily flights to nearly 150 destinations.
source_title: What Happened To Delta Air Lines' Hub In Cincinnati?
supporting_excerpt: At its peak in 2005, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) was Delta Airline's second largest hub, offering more than 600 flights per day to nearly 150 destinations... In 2005, CVG processed over 22.7 million passengers.
caveat: Trade publication; consistent with CVG official statistics.

claim: By 2013, CVG offered fewer than 180 daily departures to 77 destinations and processed fewer than 6 million passengers per year; by 2014 it had fallen to 54th busiest US airport by enplanements.
source_title: What Happened To Delta Air Lines' Hub In Cincinnati?
supporting_excerpt: By 2013, CVG provided fewer than 180 daily departures to 77 destinations and processed fewer than 6 million passengers per year. Nine years later (2014), it was 54th on the list of busiest U.S. airports by enplanements.
caveat: Trade publication figures; consistent with FAA enplanement rankings.

claim: St. Louis Lambert reached approximately 15 million enplaned passengers in 2000 with TWA carrying 71% of them; American acquired TWA's assets in 2001.
source_title: What Happened To American Airlines' Hub In St. Louis?
supporting_excerpt: The airport reaching 15 million enplaned passengers in 2000 (TWA accounted for 71% of passengers in that year). In 2001 TWA declared bankruptcy for the third time, which resulted in American Airlines acquiring TWA's assets.
caveat: Trade publication figures; consistent with historical STL statistics.

claim: American Airlines cut STL daily services from 417 to 207 in 2003, cutting an additional 210 flights that year and driving passenger counts below 14 million.
source_title: What Happened To American Airlines' Hub In St. Louis?
supporting_excerpt: By the end of 2002, American Airlines had removed nearly 20% of its daily flights, and, in 2003, American Airlines cut its 417 daily services to just 207. In 2003 American slashed 210 more flights out of Lambert as passenger counts plummeted to under 14 million.
caveat: Trade publication figures.

claim: United announced closure of its Cleveland Hopkins hub on February 1, 2014, stating the hub 'hasn't been profitable for over a decade'; departures fell from ~200 to 72 and destinations from 61 to 20.
source_title: What Happened To United Airlines' Cleveland Hub?
supporting_excerpt: On February 1, 2014, United announced that the airline would shut down its Cleveland hub, stating that the airline's hub at Cleveland 'hasn't been profitable for over a decade.'... daily departures dropped from nearly 200 to 72... the destination count went from 61 to 20.
caveat: Trade publication figures.

claim: Concourse D at Cleveland Hopkins — built for the hub — has sat empty since May 2014 when United shut its hub operation.
source_title: There are Both Positive and Negative Outcomes from Cleveland Hopkins Airport De-hubbing
supporting_excerpt: Concourse 'D' at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport has sat empty since May of 2014 when United Airlines shut-down its hub.
caveat: Public-radio secondary source.

claim: Detroit's McNamara Terminal opened February 24, 2002, designed for Northwest Airlines' Detroit hub as a linear midfield with satellite concourses.
source_title: The cost and reasons for building Northwest's DTW WorldGateway in 2000-2002
supporting_excerpt: The McNamara Terminal, also once known as the Northwest WorldGateway, opened February 24, 2002... designed to accommodate Northwest's hub operation.
caveat: Forum source; opening date corroborated by DTW airport publications.

claim: Atlanta's Maynard H. Jackson Jr. International Terminal (including Concourse F) opened May 16, 2012 at a total cost of $1.4 billion, with 12 international gates on Concourse F.
source_title: Maynard H. Jackson Jr. International Terminal, Atlanta, Georgia
supporting_excerpt: The new international terminal opened at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on May 16, 2012... The total cost of building the new terminal was $1.4 billion... Concourse F having 12 gates.
caveat: Trade publication figures.

claim: JetBlue opened Terminal 5i, a $200 million international arrivals extension at JFK Terminal 5, in November 2014 — six years after T5 opened.
source_title: JetBlue Airways Opens International Arrivals Concourse at Its Award-Winning Terminal 5 at John F. Kennedy International Airport
supporting_excerpt: JetBlue Airways Opens International Arrivals Concourse at Its Award-Winning Terminal 5 at John F. Kennedy International Airport.
caveat: Primary corporate release; construction cost figure of $200M sourced additionally to Airport Technology and Turner Construction.

claim: JetBlue is investing an additional ~$100 million in a 2025-2026 refresh of JFK Terminal 5, including a new BlueHouse premium lounge.
source_title: JetBlue unveils $100M Terminal 5 transformation at JFK Airport
supporting_excerpt: JetBlue unveils $100M Terminal 5 transformation at JFK Airport.
caveat: Regional press; corroborated by JetBlue investor communications.

claim: The Passenger Facility Charge cap was raised to $4.50 per enplaning passenger in 2001 under the Wendell H. Ford Aviation Investment and Reform Act (AIR-21) and has been unchanged since.
source_title: Passenger facility charge
supporting_excerpt: Effective 2001, due to passage of the Wendell H. Ford Aviation Investment and Reform Act for the 21st Century, Congress raised the PFC cap to $4.50 per ticket or $18 per round trip.
denominator: per enplaning passenger; max 2 per one-way, 4 per round trip
caveat: Underlying primary law is 49 U.S.C. § 40117 as amended by AIR-21 (Pub. L. 106-181).

claim: Reason Foundation's 2020 policy analysis of PFC modernization concluded that construction-cost inflation since 2001 has substantially eroded the real value of the $4.50 cap.
source_title: Modernizing the Passenger Facility Charge for Aviation Recovery
supporting_excerpt: Reason Foundation policy paper on modernizing the Passenger Facility Charge.
caveat: Advocacy-adjacent policy source; use for framing, not for a specific dollar-erosion figure.

claim: American Airlines' new Boeing 787-9 configuration reduces total seats from 285 to 244, increases lie-flat business class from 30 to 51 seats, and increases premium economy from 21 to 32 seats.
source_title: Can American Airlines Close The Profit Gap With Delta & United?
supporting_excerpt: American's newly configured Boeing 787-9 has just 244 seats compared to 285 on the older configuration, with lie-flat business class seats increasing from 30 to 51 and Premium Economy growing from 21 to 32 seats.
units: seats per aircraft by cabin class
caveat: Trade publication summary of American Airlines investor communications.

claim: American Airlines is opening the network's largest Admirals Club (~37,000 sq ft) in Terminal C at DFW and its first Flagship Check-In in Terminal D at DFW in 2026, ahead of Terminal F opening.
source_title: American Airlines Brings Flagship Check-In to DFW as It Chases Its Rivals
supporting_excerpt: American Airlines will open the largest Admirals Club in its network and introduce dedicated Flagship check-in at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW)... a new 37,000-square-foot lounge in Terminal C and its first Flagship check-in facility in Terminal D in 2026.
caveat: Trade press; also referenced in the airport context packet.
